table.text: Patients and caregivers were recruited from the outpatient waiting list.
Written informed consent was obtained before participation.

Participants completed two adapted versions: one assessing the usability of the tool m-Path as an app (e.g., 'I think I would like to use this tool frequently') and one assessing the dashboard visualizing ESM data (e.g., 'I think I would like to use this dashboard frequently').
Four participants met the adherence criterion (50%), reaching the predefined threshold.
The remaining participants were treated by nine therapists (M = 32.3 yrs, SD = 6.5, range = 27-46).
Only three participants were born outside Germany.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: to support case conceptualization, treatment monitoring, and feedback.
Combined with single-case experimental designs (SCED), this allows casual inferences about intervention effects for the individual.
However, implementation remains challenging.
This study aimed to prepare for the implementation of an ESM based SCED infrastructure in an outpatient university-affiliated psychotherapy setting.
We conducted a preregistered mixed-methods feasibility study with adult and adolescent patients, caregivers, and therapists.

Across three iterative SCED phases (baseline, diagnostic, intervention), patients and caregivers completed two-week daily time-contingent ESM surveys with optional eventcontingent surveys and boosters.
Usability, acceptability, adherence, and compliance were assessed via questionnaires and ESM data.
Semi-structured interviews explored perceived barriers.
Usability and acceptability were generally good, but acceptability varied and tended to decline over time.
Adherence fell below the predefined criterion, whereas compliance among adherent participants generally met the criterion, except in adolescents.
Perceived burden was low, but perceived helpfulness limited.

Interviews revealed distinct barriers: Patients and caregivers mainly reported gaps in reflecting personal experiences, followed by response burden and challenges integrating assessments into daily life.
Therapists mainly reported limited resources, limited utility to guide change, and uncertainty in interpreting data.
These findings may inform strategies for implementing ESM-based SCED systems in routine care.
Future work should focus on enhancing personalization of assessments and addressing limited therapist resources to support clinical integration.
A key challenge remains ensuring that the ESM-based SCED infrastructure is perceived not as an administrative burden, but as a tool that meaningfully enhances therapeutic processes.

Measurement-based care (MBC), also known as routine-outcome monitoring (ROM) or feedback-informed treatment, involves (a) routinely collecting patient data on symptoms, outcomes, or processes, (b) providing feedback to the therapist, (c) reviewing this information with the patient, and (d) collaboratively adjusting the treatment plan as needed (Lutz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Measurement-based care (MBC), also known as routine-outcome monitoring (ROM) or feedback-informed treatment, involves (a) routinely collecting patient data on symptoms, outcomes, or processes, (b) providing feedback to the therapist, (c) reviewing this information with the patient, and (d) collaboratively adjusting the treatment plan as needed <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lutz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Systematic reviews have demonstrated modest, incremental improvements in treatment outcomes (g ≈ 0.15), with larger effects when clinical support tools are implemented in cases of insufficient treatment response (g ≈ 0.36-0.53) (Barkham et al., 2023; de Jong et al., 2021).

text.text: Recent technical innovations are shaping new developments in MBC.

While data are typically collected at each consultation, intensive longitudinal data approaches, such as ambulatory assessment, experience sampling, and ecological momentary assessment, are increasingly employed (Myin-Germeys et al., 2024).
text.formatted: While data are typically collected at each consultation, intensive longitudinal data approaches, such as ambulatory assessment, experience sampling, and ecological momentary assessment, are increasingly employed <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Myin-Germeys et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These enable even deeper integration of data into cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) treatments, for example by improving case conceptualization (Scholten et al., 2022) or supporting self-monitoring or therapeutic homework assignments through interactive feedback systems (Bringmann et al., 2025).

text.text: Traditionally, MBC has relied on comparison between individual patient data and a reference group for interpretation.

By incorporating single-case experimental designs, in which an individual provides baseline data as reference and the start of an intervention is randomized, changes can be attributed more confidently to the intervention itself rather than to external factors such as seasonal variation or spontaneous recovery (Vlaeyen et al., 2020).

text.text: In clinical practice, the aim is less to isolate causal variables than to apply the logic of such designs to identify and monitor maladaptive mechanisms and treatment targets, and to test whether these change in response to treatment, thereby guiding treatment planning and improving therapeutic change for an individual patient (Kazdin, 2019).

text.text: Despite the benefits of MBC, its implementation in routine practice faces significant barriers (Barkham et al., 2023; Deane et al., 2024).

text.text: For example, in a survey of 159 providers across three U.S. youth mental health care services (Jensen-Doss et al., 2025), MBC measures were administered to only 40-60% of patients on average.

text.text: Related practices, such as reviewing scores and graphs, discussing results in supervision, providing feedback to patients, and using results to inform treatment planning, were reported at even lower rates, falling in the 1-39% range.

Implementation frameworks emphasize the importance of understanding the factors that influence adoption at multiple levels, including patient and provider characteristics, organizational context, and the broader healthcare system in which mental health care is delivered (Damschroder et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2025).

text.text: To date, MBC has primarily been studied in Western healthcare systems within outpatient or counseling settings (de Jong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To date, MBC has primarily been studied in Western healthcare systems within outpatient or counseling settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(de Jong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In these contexts, a recent systematic review of 23 quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods studies found that patients and providers value MBC for enhancing communication, improving insight, and supporting more structured data-based treatment planning (Dey et al., 2025).

text.text: Yet, the review also identified several concerns that might hinder uptake, including limited ability to capture clinical complexity, potential reporting biases, negative effects on the therapeutic alliance, time constraints, insufficient training, unclear guidance for interpretation, and issues related to data use and privacy.

Although intensive longitudinal data may address some concerns, for example, by providing a more accurate, real-time representation of a patient's experience in daily life, some challenges such as insufficient training and unclear guidance for data interpretation may persist or even intensify, as suggested by qualitative findings (De Thurah et al., 2025; Weermeijer et al., 2023).

text.text: Given these barriers, it is recommended to employ implementation strategies when introducing MBC into a specific setting (Lewis et al., 2019; Whitmyre et al., 2024).

text.text: This feasibility study had two aims.
The first aim was to evaluate the feasibility of an ESMbased SCED infrastructure for MBC in an outpatient university setting.

Feasibility was assessed through iterative rounds of testing, with findings from each round informing subsequent refinements of the infrastructure in accordance with the principles of agile research (Wilson et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Feasibility was assessed through iterative rounds of testing, with findings from each round informing subsequent refinements of the infrastructure in accordance with the principles of agile research <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wilson et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The second aim was to identify and explore perceived barriers to the implementation of the infrastructure and to use these insights to inform the refinement subsequent implementation strategies.
The study was conducted as part of the preparation for the broader implementation of the infrastructure in a subsequent pilot phase (Scholten et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The study was conducted as part of the preparation for the broader implementation of the infrastructure in a subsequent pilot phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Scholten et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to iterative optimization, stakeholder engagement constituted a second key implementation principle, with stakeholders being actively involved throughout the development process to ensure that the infrastructure addressed their needs (Chinsen et al., 2025; Manafò et al., 2018).

text.text: Details of the stakeholder engagement are reported elsewhere (Herzog et al., submitted).

text.text: Beyond this specific implementation context, the study contributes to emerging research on barriers to MBC implementation, particularly recent innovations leveraging intensive longitudinal data (De Thurah et al., 2025; Dey et al., 2025; Soyster et al., 2023; Weermeijer et al., 2023).

text.text: This feasibility study employed a single-site, non-randomized design.
The primary focus was to implement and evaluate the feasibility of the infrastructure with adult patients and therapists.

Quantitative feasibility outcomes were collected at three time points (post-baseline, post-diagnostic, and approximately six weeks after intervention start) complemented by qualitative semi-structured interviews across two successive cohorts.
Key changes between cohorts included the introduction of individualized items and clearer variable labels to improve visualization interpretability.
Ultimately, the procedures were deemed appropriate for a one-year pilot study.
An additional iteration with adolescents, caregivers, and therapists assessed the infrastructure's applicability across age groups.
Key changes included adapting the ESM survey to adolescents' needs.

The entire implementation process was ethically approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology at the RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau (#LEK-535) and outlined in a previously published study protocol (Scholten et al., 2024).

text.text: A detailed analysis plan has been preregistered in the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8k5cj).
text.formatted: A detailed analysis plan has been preregistered in the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/8k5cj">https://osf.io/8k5cj</ref>).

text.text: Guidelines for implementation feasibility studies were followed (Pearson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Guidelines for implementation feasibility studies were followed <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Pearson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The study was conducted at the outpatient clinic of the Department of Psychology at the RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau, which has a treatment unit for adults and a unit for children and adolescents.
The adult unit has approximately 250 new admissions per year.
A wide range of diagnoses are treated, with the three main diagnoses being depression, anxiety, and adjustment disorders.
The unit for children and adolescents also has approximately 250 new admissions per year, with the three main diagnoses being anxiety, depression, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
In the youth unit, caregivers are regularly involved in treatment (usually every fourth session on average), depending on the age of patients.
Both units train students after their master's degree to become licensed psychotherapists with a focus on CBT.
Trainees receive theoretical input and regular supervision from licensed psychotherapists.
Both units are also regularly involved in recruiting and treating patients for clinical trials.
Common diagnostic procedures in both units include an intake interview by a licensed psychotherapist and the administration of a structured clinical interview.
General and disorder-specific questionnaires are administered at intake, during the diagnostic phase, every 10 therapy sessions, at the end of treatment and at the 6-month follow-up.
In the unit for adults, the Symptom Checklist 90 (SCL-90; Franke, 2014) is used as indicator for general mental health problems.

The unit for children and adolescents uses the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL 6-18R; Döpfner et al., 2014), the Youth Self Report (YSR 11-18R; Döpfner et al., 2014) and, for research purposes, the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ, self-and parent-report; Goodman, 1997).
text.formatted: The unit for children and adolescents uses the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL 6-18R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Döpfner et al., 2014)</ref>, the Youth Self Report (YSR 11-18R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Döpfner et al., 2014)</ref> and, for research purposes, the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ, self-and parent-report; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Goodman, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The ESM-based SCED infrastructure is integrated into this existing routine diagnostic process.
Patients and caregivers were recruited from the outpatient waiting list.
Only patients and caregivers who agreed to be contacted for research studies were called by research assistants.
Upon starting therapy, the therapist was also contacted.
During the telephone call, individuals were informed of the purpose and procedure of the feasibility study.
Written informed consent was obtained before participation.
Individuals could decide independently whether to participate in the study.

As we plan to apply the ESM-based SCED infrastructure to all outpatients in the future, we did not formulate specific inclusion criteria, but only excluded people with severe mental health problems, such as acute psychosis or suicidal tendencies.
Adolescents could participate at the age of 12 and above.
In line with previous studies (Bartels et al., 2022), we aimed to recruit 6-12 patient-therapist dyads per cohort, a sample size considered sufficient to provide estimates with adequate precision.
text.formatted: In line with previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bartels et al., 2022)</ref>, we aimed to recruit 6-12 patient-therapist dyads per cohort, a sample size considered sufficient to provide estimates with adequate precision.

text.text: This sample size is also consistent with recommendations for interview studies (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022).
text.formatted: This sample size is also consistent with recommendations for interview studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hennink & Kaiser, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The ESM-based SCED infrastructure is designed to complement traditional diagnostic methods with additional ESM surveys.

Beyond information on symptoms and functioning, this approach is intended to provide additional day-to-day insight into treatment changes while empowering patients, supporting self-management, promoting goal-directed assessment and shared decision-making (Myin-Germeys et al., 2024), fostering therapist self-reflection in line with the scientist-practitioner model (Kazdin, 2019), and generating longitudinal data for broader research (Wright & Zimmermann, 2019).
text.formatted: Beyond information on symptoms and functioning, this approach is intended to provide additional day-to-day insight into treatment changes while empowering patients, supporting self-management, promoting goal-directed assessment and shared decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Myin-Germeys et al., 2024)</ref>, fostering therapist self-reflection in line with the scientist-practitioner model <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kazdin, 2019)</ref>, and generating longitudinal data for broader research <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wright & Zimmermann, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As emotion regulation is considered to be an important transdiagnostic mechanism (Bjureberg, 2026; Palmieri et al., 2022), an ESM survey was developed to assess different aspects of emotion regulation (Kolb-Grunder et al., submitted).
text.formatted: As emotion regulation is considered to be an important transdiagnostic mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bjureberg, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Palmieri et al., 2022)</ref>, an ESM survey was developed to assess different aspects of emotion regulation <ref type="bibr">(Kolb-Grunder et al., submitted)</ref>.

text.text: We selected this standardized set of measures to simplify implementation and support automatization.

Based on stakeholder input, an additional interview guide informed the formulation of problem-and goal-focused idiographic ESM measures for each patient in the second adult cohort (Galden et al., in preparation).
text.formatted: Based on stakeholder input, an additional interview guide informed the formulation of problem-and goal-focused idiographic ESM measures for each patient in the second adult cohort <ref type="bibr">(Galden et al., in preparation)</ref>.

text.text: The ESM protocol was developed collaboratively between the research team and patient and therapist stakeholders, based on systematic guidelines for methodological decision-making in ESM studies (Janssens et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The ESM protocol was developed collaboratively between the research team and patient and therapist stakeholders, based on systematic guidelines for methodological decision-making in ESM studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Janssens et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The ESM survey was administered at the end of the day, with semi-random beeps scheduled during a personalized evening time frame.

Participants could also use additional event-based surveys to report on relevant situations using a home button which triggers a measurement burst with five follow-up surveys within the next hour to monitor mood.
The m-Path software was chosen for its user-friendly ESM data collection and its flexible visualization of patient responses (Mestdagh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The m-Path software was chosen for its user-friendly ESM data collection and its flexible visualization of patient responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Mestdagh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The research team initially proposed the SCED procedure based on the Risk of Bias in N-of-1 Trials (RoBiNT) scale, a scale for assessing the methodological rigor of SCED studies (Tate et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The research team initially proposed the SCED procedure based on the Risk of Bias in N-of-1 Trials (RoBiNT) scale, a scale for assessing the methodological rigor of SCED studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Tate et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Research assistants supported the onboarding phase by helping participants log into m-Path, introducing the ESM survey using handouts, and presenting sample dashboards to enhance compliance.

Within the SCED framework, ESM surveys were administered for two weeks following the first appointment (Phase A: baseline), during diagnostic sessions (Phase B: diagnostics), and during initial treatment sessions (Phase C: intervention).
After each SCED phase, research assistants created individualized dashboards (the equivalent of mood bars in m-Path) that were discussed with patients, caregivers, and therapists.
Our intention was for participants to actively use m-Path, for example, to discuss critical situations, reflect on coping patterns, and monitor therapeutic change goals.
Quantitative feasibility outcomes measures were administered via SoSci Survey (Leiner, 2024).
text.formatted: Quantitative feasibility outcomes measures were administered via SoSci Survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Leiner, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therapists completed feasibility outcome assessments for each patient separately, as their perceptions of feasibility could vary across patients.
To obtain a balanced assessment, participants who had discontinued diagnostic procedures were also encouraged to provide ratings of their experience.

text.text: It was applied here to systematically identify perceived barriers and inform implementation strategies.
An inductive approach was used to capture the user experience.
The analysis followed several steps.
First, the research question was defined ('What barriers do patients (including caregivers) and therapists experience when going through the ESM-based SCED procedures?').
Second, interviews were automatically transcribed using MAXQDA's AI-supported transcription (VERBI Software GmbH, 2025) and checked for accuracy.
Third, the first author (LS) reviewed the first cohort and generated initial coding ideas.
Fourth, this preliminary system was applied to data from subsequent cohorts by a research assistant trained by the first author, with notes on required refinements.
Based on these notes, the initial category system was collaboratively refined through discussion.
Fifth, the final category system was agreed upon through consensus and applied to the full dataset by the research assistant.
Thirty percent of the interviews were double-coded by the first author, allowing for the assessment of interrater agreement.
AI-assisted English paraphrases of the German transcripts were used to illustrate category descriptions.
The authors reviewed these paraphrases and take full responsibility for their accuracy and fidelity to the original German content.

Finally, category frequencies were analyzed separately for patients (including caregivers) and therapists to explore differences in perceived barriers and inform more targeted implementation strategies.
Both coders were White women with a background in clinical psychology and prior involvement in the implementation project.
The research assistant was a master's student in clinical psychology, while the first author was a postdoctoral clinical researcher and licensed CBT psychotherapist.
Throughout the coding process, they met regularly to discuss discrepancies, clarify coding decisions, and align their interpretation of the coding scheme.
Given their prior involvement in the project, they also reflected on whether their perspectives might have led them to perceive implementation barriers less critically.

A total of 45 interviews were conducted: 20 with patients, 7 with caregivers, and 18 with therapists.

Of these, two interviews were conducted with patients and one interview was conducted with a caregiver who discontinued diagnostic procedures and reported barriers, including reasons for discontinuation and treatment-related dissatisfaction.

Median interview duration was comparable across patients (8:43 min, range = 3:27-16:29) and therapists (9:34 min, range = 5:40-15:59), while interviews with caregivers were somewhat longer (11:26 min, range = 10:42-23:54).
Intercoder reliability was substantial (κ = .77).
Based on the interviews, 21 categories were developed inductively and organized into two main categories, each comprising three subcategories.
The first main category captured barriers related to responding to the daily questions and was reported predominantly by patients.
The second main category concerned challenges associated with integrating the results of the daily assessments into psychotherapy and was reported primarily by therapists.

text.text: Aiming to prepare for broader implementation, the present study examined the feasibility of an ESM-based SCED infrastructure for MBC and explored perceived barriers.
Overall, usability and acceptability were good and comparable across adult and child/adolescent units, supporting implementation in both settings.
However, acceptability was not consistent across all time points and showed a tendency to decline over the course of treatment, particularly in the first adult cohort.

While adherence across SCED phases was below the predefined criterion for adult patients and caregivers, compliance among adherent patients and caregivers met the criterion, except for the adolescent group.
Perceived burden rated at the end of each ESM survey was low, whereas perceived helpfulness was limited.

Qualitative data provided by interviews revealed distinct barriers from a patient and therapist perspective: Patients and caregivers primarily reported barriers to responding, with difficulties in reflecting on personal experiences most frequently mentioned, followed by response burden and challenges of integrating responses into daily life.
Therapists, in contrast, mainly reported barriers to treatment integration, most frequently limited resources, as well as limited utility for guiding change and uncertainty in interpretation.

Consistent with broader critiques from a patient perspective that standard MBC instruments inadequately capture clinical complexity and subjective experiences (Dey et al., 2025), patients and caregivers in the present feasibility trial most frequently reported difficulties in reflecting personal experiences as a key barrier, when using a standardized ESM survey and schedule.

text.text: An interesting observation was that, after introducing individualized items and clearer variable labels in the second adult cohort, acceptability seemed to have slightly improved.

This suggests that individualizing ESM assessments may increase motivation and clinical relevance, consistent with recommendations for greater personalization from patients and clinicians in previous studies on the use of ESM in clinical practice (Bos et al., 2019; Piot et al., 2022; Weermeijer et al., 2023).

text.text: While some limitations may be easily addressed, for example by extending the response time window, patient feedback in interviews suggested that burden may also be outweighed by increasing perceived benefit, for instance through integrating collected data into therapy sessions to promote insight and awareness, but also to discuss and derive concrete action steps together with the therapist for dealing with burdensome everyday situations.
In contrast, completing the ESM survey alone was unsurprisingly perceived as of limited usefulness.

From a therapist perspective, the main barrier to treatment integration was a lack of resources, including time, workload, technical infrastructure, and potential interference with more important treatment goals, consistent with reported barriers to MBC in general (Dey et al., 2025) and ESM in particular (Piot et al., 2022; Soyster et al., 2023; Weermeijer et al., 2023).

text.text: Thus, to reduce therapist burden and facilitate treatment integration, we complemented automated time series and other visualizations (e.g., word clouds and phase comparisons) with therapeutic questions as headings and brief descriptions to enhance their clinical meaningfulness for use in the subsequent implementation trial.

Despite this relatively simple automated solution, a key challenge remains to ensure that the ESMbased SCED infrastructure is not experienced as an additional administrative burden but as a tool that meaningfully supports the therapeutic process.

In this regard, our findings also underscore the importance of training therapists in the use of such ESM-based SCED systems, in line with previous studies (Dey et al., 2025; Piot et al., 2022; Soyster et al., 2023; Weermeijer et al., 2023).

text.text: Accordingly, our future implementation trials will place particular emphasis on therapist engagement: Beyond mandatory introductory training, we offer additional free supervision and technical support, modest financial compensation for the additional workload, and assistance with digitizing existing worksheets for integration into the predefined ESM-based SCED procedure.

Especially through personal exchange with therapists during training and supervision, we see an opportunity to address individual concerns and barriers while drawing on their hands-on experience to explore patient-specific applications.
Beyond monitoring treatment progress, ESM-based SCED may offer broader opportunities for MBC.
For example, these tools could support different CBT modules through feedback systems, facilitate self-monitoring, and enable the evaluation of homework assignments (Bringmann et al., 2025).

text.text: We hope that these implementation strategies will not only facilitate therapist uptake but also indirectly promote sustained patient engagement throughout treatment.
Several limitations merit attention.

First, a key limitation is that, although feasibility was assessed in both an adult and a child/adolescent unit, the adult patient sample was relatively young (range 23-56) and thus do not capture barriers that may be experienced by older adults.
Only three participants were born outside Germany.
Thus, potential language-related or other culture-related barriers could not be examined.
Similarly, the spectrum of mental health conditions was not fully represented.

For the planned implementation trial, these aspects can be systematically addressed to examine whether and how the ESM-based SCED infrastructure needs to be adapted for broader and more heterogeneous clinical populations.

Second, because the perspectives of individuals who discontinued the diagnostic procedure are particularly relevant for understanding barriers, we retained their data in the quantitative analyses and invited them to participate in the interviews.
Nevertheless, only three of twelve individuals agreed to be interviewed.
In addition, the perspectives of therapists who declined participation at the beginning, despite patients being willing to participate, are lacking.
Third, as the ESM-based SCED infrastructure was new to all participants, research assistants supported each patient-therapist dyad in implementation and technical issues.

However, this sometimes led to role ambiguity regarding whether the system was part of the study or routine therapy, including uncertainty about how results should be integrated into treatment, which may partly explain lower adherence rates.

Fourth, as both units serve as training clinics, the therapists included in this study were relatively early in their professional career and may not fully represent therapists in routine clinical care.
Future feasibility and implementation studies in non-university settings and other health care systems are therefore essential to study and facilitate broader implementation of MBC.
Overall, ESM-based SCED implementation appears feasible, but maintaining perceived acceptability and utility throughout treatment remains essential.
Two key levers emerged that might support implementation, with potential relevance beyond our particular context.

For patients, daily assessments may be more acceptable when they are personally meaningful, flexible, and clearly linked to the therapeutic process, helping to balance response burden with perceived benefit.

For therapists, beyond initial training in using the ESM-based SCED infrastructure, implementation efforts may benefit from addressing limited resources and enabling ongoing exchange to discuss patient-specific applications.

A central challenge in implementation appears ensuring that the ESM-based SCED infrastructure is perceived not as an additional administrative burden but as a tool that meaningfully supports the therapeutic process.
